*Aust. J. Bot.*, 1983, **31**, 293-6

### **Relationship between Time Since the Last Fire and Flowering in** *Telopea speciosissima* **R. Br. and** *Lambertia formosa* **Sm.**

*Graham H. Pyke*

The Australian Museum, 6-8 College St, Sydney, N.S.W., 2000.

#### *Abstract*

For *Telopea speciosissima* the percentage (or density) of plants in flower, the average number of flowers per inflorescence and the average number of fruits per inflorescence all appear to peak 2 years after a summer fire and decline thereafter. On the other hand, the average height of the inflorescences above the ground increases with time since the last fire. For *Lambertia formosa* the density of inflorescences appears to reach a peak 2 or 3 years after a summer fire.

#### **Introduction**

The effects of fire on the Australian flora are many and are increasingly well studied (see Gill *et al.* 1981). There appears, however, to be little quantitative information on the relationships between time since the last fire and flowering of Australian plants (Gill 1981; Specht 1981). Only for *Xanthorrhoea australis* is there a well established relationship (Specht *et al.* 1958; Garnet 1971; Gill and Ingwersen 1976; Gill 1981): in some places this species flowers only rarely in the absence of fire (Specht *et al.* 1958; Garnet 1971).

The aim of this paper is to analyse spatial and temporal variation in flowering of *Telopea speciosissima* (waratah) and *Lambertia formosa* with respect to time since the last fire. This analysis is possible as a result of studies on the pollination biology of these plants and the foraging ecology of honeyeaters that visit them for nectar (Pyke 1980, 1981*a*, 1981*b*).

#### **Methods**

The data presented were collected between December 1979 and December 1981 in the Brisbane Water National Park (lat. 33°32′22″S., long. 151°16′56″E.; elevation 170 m above sea level) and Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park (lat. 33°36′18″S., long. 151°16′16″E.; elevation 145 m above sea level). In each region, study sites are located in plateau-type, low open-forest (Benson and Fallding 1981) dominated by *Eucalyptus gummifera* (Gaertn.) Hochr., *E. haemastoma* Sm. and *E. oblonga* DC., with a shrub understory composed mainly of *Lambertia formosa* Sm. Both regions are located on plateau tops and hence all study sites have the same aspect. In both regions soils are deep, yellow and earthy (Benson and Fallding 1981) with no apparent differences between the study sites.

The Brisbane Water study site contains two areas in terms of fire history: one area last burnt in December 1976, the other in December 1979. The two areas are separated by a vehicle trail which stopped the more recent fire from spreading further. There are no apparent differences between the two areas in terms of soil or vegetation. The entire Ku-ring-gai Chase study site last burnt in 1965.

Flowering in *Telopea speciosissima* has been recorded in two ways. In the 1976 burn study area in Brisbane Water National Park, the total number of flowering plants was recorded for the spring flowering periods of 1979, 1980 and 1981. For each inflorescence

0067-1924/83/030293$02.00


<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

294 G. H. Pyke

the total number of flowers, height above the ground and number of fruits were also recorded. In each year peak flowering occurred about mid September with high synchrony among plants. In this area and in the other two study areas, permanent circular plots of 20 m radius were established and the numbers of flowering plants within these circles counted every 3 weeks during spring 1981. The numbers of non-flowering plants in each circle were also recorded for spring 1981. Flowering in *Lambertia formosa* was recorded by counting the number of inflorescences in each circle during spring 1981 and in two of the present Brisbane Water circles during spring 1980. During spring 1981, there were four circles in the Brisbane Water area of the 1976 fire, two in the area of the 1979 fire and two in the Ku-ring-gai Chase area.

#### **Results**

#### *Flowering of* Telopea *in Successive Years*

In the Brisbane Water area which last burnt in December 1976, the total number of flowering *Telopea* plants has declined dramatically since spring 1979 (Table 1). Since spring

**Table 1. Flowering of** ***Telopea speciosissima*** **in areas of 1976 and 1979 fires during successive years**

| Area | Flowering time | Total No. of flowering plants | Mean No. of flowers per inflorescence | Mean inflorescence ht (cm) | Mean No. of fruit per inflorescence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1976 fire | Spring 1979 | 306 | 79·5±0·9 | 162·4±2·5 | 2·45±0·11 |
| | Spring 1980 | 100 | 64·9±1·4 | 186·0±3·4 | 0·86±0·11 |
| | Spring 1981 | 9 | 62·3±3·0 | 228·8±13·3 | 0·56±0·24 |
| | | Sample size | | | |
| 1979 fire | Spring 1981 | 63 | 171·8±4·2 | 138·7±3·1 | 3·74±0·41 |

1979 there have also been decreases in the average number of flowers per inflorescence and in the average number of fruit per inflorescence and increases in the average inflorescence height. The differences between 1979 and 1980 are all significant (*P*<0·05, *t*-test); for 1980 and 1981 only the difference in mean inflorescence height is significant (*P*<0·05, *t*-test). During spring 1981 in the circles in the 1979 fire area (see Table 1), the inflorescence height averaged less than for any of the flowering periods in the 1976 fire area (*P*<0·05, *t*-test) while the numbers of flowers and fruits per inflorescence averaged more (*P*<0·05, *t*-test).

#### *Flowering of* Telopea *in Different Places*

During spring 1981 the density of flowering plants (i.e. number of flowering plants per circle) and the percentage of plants in flower declined with increases in the time since an area last burnt (Table 2). The differences in the percentage of flowering are significant between the 1979 and 1976 (or 1965) burn areas (*P*<0·05, *t*-test based on Normal approximation to binomial) but not between the 1965 and 1976 burn areas (*P*>0·05, *t*-test based on Normal approximation to binomial).

#### *Flowering of* Lambertia

During spring 1981 the peak density of *Lambertia* inflorescences declined with increases in the time since an area last burnt (Table 3). The differences between the areas are significantly different (*P*<0·05 for comparisons between 1979 and 1976 burn areas and between 1976 and 1965 burn areas, *t*-test).

For two circles in the 1976 burn area, the peak numbers of *Lambertia* inflorescences declined significantly from spring 1980 to spring 1981 (*P*<0·05, *t*-test) (Table 3).


<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

Fire and Flowering in *Telopea* and *Lambertia* 295

#### **Discussion**

There appear to be strong relationships between flowering and time since the last fire for both *Telopea* and *Lambertia*. In the case of *Telopea*, the percentage (or density) of plants in flower, the average number of flowers per inflorescence and the average number of fruits per inflorescence all peak 2 years after a summer fire and decline thereafter (Tables 1 and 2). On the other hand, the average height of the inflorescences above the ground appears to increase with increases in time since the last fire (Table 1). This undoubtedly reflects the continual growth of the plants, starting from a rhizome, following a fire. The density of *Lambertia* inflorescences reaches a peak 2 or 3 years after a summer fire (Table 3). No information is currently available on either the cause or the adaptive significance of these relationships.

**Table 2. Flowering of** ***Telopea speciosissima*** **in different areas during spring 1981**

| Area | No. of circles | Mean No. of flowering plants per circle | Mean No. of plants per circle | Percentage of plants in flower |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ku-ring-gai Chase (1965 fire) | 2 | 0·50 | 32·5±5·5 | 1·5 (*n*=65) |
| Brisbane Water (1976 fire) | 4 | 0·75 | 138·8±19·4 | 0·5 (*n*=555) |
| Brisbane Water (1979 fire) | 2 | 23·00 | 105·0±2·0 | 22·0 (*n*=210) |

**Table 3. Flowering of** ***Lambertia formosa*** **in different areas during spring 1980 and 1981**

| Area | Peak No. of inflorescences per circle: 1980 Mean | 1980 s.e. | 1980 *n* | 1981 Mean | 1981 s.e. | 1981 *n* |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ku-ring-gai Chase (1965 fire) | — | — | — | 5·5 | 3·5 | 2 |
| Brisbane Water (1976 fire) | 195·5 | 17·5 | 2 | 96·5 | 7·8 | 4 |
| Brisbane Water (1979 fire) | — | — | — | 419·0 | 108·0 | 2 |

National Parks and Wildlife Service. Two anonymous referees provided many helpful comments on an earlier version of this paper.

- Gill, A. M. (1981). Adaptive responses of Australian vascular plant species to fires. *In* 'Fire and the Australian Biota', eds A. M. Gill, R. H. Groves and I. R. Noble. (Aust. Acad. Sci.: Canberra.)

The differences in the percentage of flowering are significant between the 1979 and 1976 (or 1965) burn areas (*P*<0·05, *t*-test based on Normal approximation to binomial) but not between the 1965 and 1976 burn areas (*P*>0·05, *t*-test based on Normal approximation to binomial).

#### *Flowering of* Lambertia

During spring 1981 the peak density of *Lambertia* inflorescences declined with increases in the time since an area last burnt (Table 3). The differences between the areas are significantly different (*P*<0·05 for comparisons between 1979 and 1976 burn areas and between 1976 and 1965 burn areas, *t*-test).

For two circles in the 1976 burn area, the peak numbers of *Lambertia* inflorescences declined significantly from spring 1980 to spring 1981 (*P*<0·05, *t*-test) (Table 3).


<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

Fire and Flowering in *Telopea* and *Lambertia* 295

#### **Discussion**

There appear to be strong relationships between flowering and time since the last fire for both *Telopea* and *Lambertia*. In the case of *Telopea*, the percentage (or density) of plants in flower, the average number of flowers per inflorescence and the average number of fruits per inflorescence all peak 2 years after a summer fire and decline thereafter (Tables 1 and 2). On the other hand, the average height of the inflorescences above the ground appears to increase with increases in time since the last fire (Table 1). This undoubtedly reflects the continual growth of the plants, starting from a rhizome, following a fire. The density of *Lambertia* inflorescences reaches a peak 2 or 3 years after a summer fire (Table 3). No information is currently available on either the cause or the adaptive significance of these relationships.

# **Secondary Succession in Post-fire Scrub Dominated by** *Acacia verticillata* **(L'Hérit.) Willd. at Wilsons Promontory, Victoria**

*David H. Ashton and Jennifer A. Chappill*

School of Botany, University of Melbourne, Parkville, Vic. 3052.

#### *Abstract*

Senescence and death of 30-year-old post-fire *Acacia verticillata* scrub in areas originally supporting sclerophyll eucalypt forest were studied over a 6-year period at Wilsons Promontory, Victoria. The potential for eucalypt regeneration was also examined. On drier sites, *A. verticillata* has been replaced by drought-resistant *Kunzea ambigua* while on wet sites it has been replaced by waterlogging-tolerant *Melaleuca ericifolia.* In mid slopes *A. verticillata* is regenerating from soil seed in gaps in the field layer of *Pteridium esculentum* and *Goodenia ovata* and forming a patchy, uneven-aged stand. The composition of the mid-slope community is determined by the relative resistance of species to browsing and grazing. The failure of eucalypts to reclaim the scrub areas at this critical time has been due to poor seed crops, seed harvesting by ants and intense selective browsing. Exclosure plots have demonstrated the importance of herbivory in modifying this vegetation and indicate potential means of reafforestation without the intervention of fire.

### **Introduction**

In the moist areas of Victoria, large areas of high forest have been converted to scrub of varying height, density and species composition by the fire regimes of the last century (Ashton 1981). Such dramatic changes have been ascribed to the fire sensitivity of the fast growing eucalypt overstorey and its relatively long non-flowering period. Thus, repeated fires at short intervals, even those of low intensity, will kill regeneration before seed has been produced. Alternatively, a similar result will be achieved if severe fires occur at a time of negligible seed storage in the crowns, or if severe drought or intense selective browsing removes or severely damages eucalypt regeneration.

The total area of potential sclerophyll forest on Wilsons Promontory (Fig. 1) is estimated to be 95 km<sup>2</sup> and includes a wide range of structure from dry to wet sclerophyll forest (Ashton 1981; Gill 1981). Much of the present forest is intermediate between these extremes and conforms to the 'damp sclerophyll' type as described by Opie *et al.* (1984). At Wilsons Promontory (Fig. 1) approximately 14% of the tall forests of *Eucalyptus obliqua* L'Hérit., *E. muelleriana* and *E. regnans*\* have been destroyed in the last 60 years by numerous fires.

Only 2·4% of the forested area currently consists of the tall open forest formation with tall and dense understoreys of shrubs, ferns and tree ferns. Of the forested areas converted to scrub, about 68% (9·0 km<sup>2</sup>) are dominated by *Acacia verticillata* in damp sclerophyll areas and 32% (4·3 km<sup>2</sup>) is dominated by *Pomaderris aspera, Bedfordia arborescens, Olearia argophylla* and *O. phlogopappa* in the wetter areas. E. obliqua is usually regarded as relatively fire resistant by virtue of its thick bark, it may be rendered susceptible if bark is depleted by repeated burning. Widespread introgression of this species with the thinner-barked E. regnans has resulted in trees with deciduous bark on the trunk and main branches; hence in many of the wetter sites, *E. obliqua* behaves as a fire-sensitive species (Smith 1970; Ashton 1981). Recent fires in the area (1927, 1939 and 1951) have produced a mosaic pattern of regeneration of the eucalypts and could have led to the development of scrub where the fires overlapped within the early non-flowering stage of the eucalypts, or where eucalypt death occurred at a time of meagre storage of capsules in the canopy, such as has occurred at Tidal River at times during the decade 1975-85. Extremely dense regeneration of *A. verticillata* in Lilly Pilly Gully followed the fires of 1951. Four years later this scrub was 2-3 m tall and virtually impenetrable. Death of stands commenced on the lower slopes and warmer aspects and by 1979-80 most stands were dead (Fig. 2c). The stems of the degenerating acacias were infested with numerous wood boring beetles, including *Notoceresium elongata* McKeown, *Pentarthrium australe* McKeown and *Menephilus coerulescens* Haag. It is possible that these and other insects have been responsible for the hastened decline of this even-aged generation. On the upper slopes, shrubs of *Kunzea ambigua* had invaded much of the degenerate scrub, whilst on the lower slopes the dominant, root-suckering species of the swamps, *Melaleuca ericifolia*, was invading much of the scrub area. The area chosen for detailed study in 1980, showed both these types of replacement. Eucalypt establishment without the intervention of fire in these communities is extremely rare.

A detailed assessment of the regeneration of the scrub began in 1979 (Chappill 1980) with the aim of predicting the future development of vegetation in these areas. The study site was near Tidal River, adjacent to the Lilly Pilly Gully walking track. The site location and the distribution of vegetation types as determined from aerial photography is indicated in Fig. 3. The study included description of the structure and species composition of the scrub, a field trial examining the possible survival of eucalypt seedlings and a survey of other species regenerating at that time.

#### **Materials and Methods**

#### *Vegetation Structure and Composition*

Floristic composition was assessed in 1983 by gathering data from 78 quadrats (10 by 2 m) along three transects from the edge of the Tidal River swamp to the *K. ambigua*-dominated scrub on the upper slopes of Mt Bishop. The pattern in these data was revealed with the aid of the computer-based hierarchical agglomerative classification program MACINF with presence and absence data (Lance and Williams 1967) and principal coordinates analysis (PCOA) of the data matrix produced by MACINF. The programs were accessed in the CSIRO TAXON package (Ross 1983).

Profiles were drawn in three representative areas to display the structure of the vegetation.

The relative areas occupied by light (<25%), medium (25-75%) and heavy (75-100%) cover classes of the field layer were assessed from intercepts on 16 lines 10 m long on the lower slopes of the degenerate scrub in 1983.

#### *Regeneration of Eucalypts in the Scrub*

An experimental plot 200 m<sup>2</sup> was chosen in a homogeneous area of typical degenerate scrub on the lower slopes (Fig. 3). It was divided into four 10 by 5 m subplots, two of which were fenced with 4 cm wire-mesh netting to a height of 1 m. The fences excluded wallabies and wombats but not possums. Seventy-two seedlings of each of the three eucalypt species which grow nearby, i. e. *E. obliqua* and *E. muelleriana*\* in the moister areas and *E. baxteri* in the drier areas, were planted in December 1979 in a random block design in three cover classes of vegetation: natural vegetation, vegetation clipped to 15 cm height in a radius of 15 cm around the seedlings and areas completely cleared of vegetation to a radius of 15 cm around the seedlings. At each spot the seedlings were assigned randomly at three points of a triangle, 10 cm apart. This resulted in 12 replications of each treatment and species combination. Seedlings were first measured on 31/12/1979 and the changes in height, growth and survival were recorded at approximately monthly intervals until mid September 1980, and then at approximately yearly intervals until 1986.

Additional plantings were made of *E. obliqua* seedlings 1-1·5 m tall in the dense vegetation surrounding the experimental plots to determine whether larger plants would be better able to establish in the scrub. Seeds of the three eucalypts were sown separately in 10 small microsites of disturbed soil 30 cm in diameter outside the plots, to evaluate the level of predation by insects or mammals on very young stages and the success of germination. All seed was lightly covered by soil, as it had been shown by A. N. Andersen (personal communication) in nearby sites that insect predation by, for example, the ants *Rhytidoponera victoreae* Andre and *Chelaner sculpturatus* Clark. could account for losses of 33-83% of the seed placed on the soil surface within 2 weeks.

The area chosen for detailed study in 1980, showed both these types of replacement. Eucalypt establishment without the intervention of fire in these communities is extremely rare.

A detailed assessment of the regeneration of the scrub began in 1979 (Chappill 1980) with the aim of predicting the future development of vegetation in these areas. The study site was near Tidal River, adjacent to the Lilly Pilly Gully walking track. The site location and the distribution of vegetation types as determined from aerial photography is indicated in Fig. 3. The study included description of the structure and species composition of the scrub, a field trial examining the possible survival of eucalypt seedlings and a survey of other species regenerating at that time.

#### **Materials and Methods**

#### *Vegetation Structure and Composition*

Floristic composition was assessed in 1983 by gathering data from 78 quadrats (10 by 2 m) along three transects from the edge of the Tidal River swamp to the *K. ambigua*-dominated scrub on the upper slopes of Mt Bishop. The pattern in these data was revealed with the aid of the computer-based hierarchical agglomerative classification program MACINF with presence and absence data (Lance and Williams 1967) and principal coordinates analysis (PCOA) of the data matrix produced by MACINF. The programs were accessed in the CSIRO TAXON package (Ross 1983).

Profiles were drawn in three representative areas to display the structure of the vegetation.

The relative areas occupied by light (<25%), medium (25-75%) and heavy (75-100%) cover classes of the field layer were assessed from intercepts on 16 lines 10 m long on the lower slopes of the degenerate scrub in 1983.

#### *Regeneration of Eucalypts in the Scrub*

An experimental plot 200 m<sup>2</sup> was chosen in a homogeneous area of typical degenerate scrub on the lower slopes (Fig. 3). It was divided into four 10 by 5 m subplots, two of which were fenced with 4 cm wire-mesh netting to a height of 1 m. The fences excluded wallabies and wombats but not possums. Seventy-two seedlings of each of the three eucalypt species which grow nearby, i. e. *E. obliqua* and *E. muelleriana*\* in the moister areas and *E. baxteri* in the drier areas, were planted in December 1979 in a random block design in three cover classes of vegetation: natural vegetation, vegetation clipped to 15 cm height in a radius of 15 cm around the seedlings and areas completely cleared of vegetation to a radius of 15 cm around the seedlings. At each spot the seedlings were assigned randomly at three points of a triangle, 10 cm apart. This resulted in 12 replications of each treatment and species combination. Seedlings were first measured on 31/12/1979 and the changes in height, growth and survival were recorded at approximately monthly intervals until mid September 1980, and then at approximately yearly intervals until 1986.

Additional plantings were made of *E. obliqua* seedlings 1-1·5 m tall in the dense vegetation surrounding the experimental plots to determine whether larger plants would be better able to establish in the scrub. Seeds of the three eucalypts were sown separately in 10 small microsites of disturbed soil 30 cm in diameter outside the plots, to evaluate the level of predation by insects or mammals on very young stages and the success of germination. All seed was lightly covered by soil, as it had been shown by A. N. Andersen (personal communication) in nearby sites that insect predation by, for example, the ants *Rhytidoponera victoreae* Andre and *Chelaner sculpturatus* Clark. could account for losses of 33-83% of the seed placed on the soil surface within 2 weeks.

# Canopy seed bank dynamics and optimum fire regime for the highly serotinous shrub, *Banksia hookeriana*

N.J. ENRIGHT,\*† BYRON B. LAMONT† and RALF MARSULA‡

\*Department of Geography and Environmental Studies, University of Melbourne, Parkville, 3052, Australia, †School of Environmental Biology, Curtin University of Technology, GPO Box U1987 Perth, 6001, Australia and ‡Sektion Ökosystemanalyse, UFZ-Umweltforschungszentrum, Leipzig-Halle GmbH, Permoserstr. 15, PF 2, 0-7050 Leipzig, Germany

#### Summary

1 *Banksia hookeriana* is a serotinous nonsprouting shrub restricted to the fire-prone northern sandplain scrub-heaths of Western Australia. Evidence of the natural fire frequency to which the species is best adapted was sought through analysis of its seed demography using a computer model of canopy seed bank dynamics based on field data.

2 Plants began flowering at 3-4 years of age but storage of viable seeds in the canopy was rare for plants < 5 years. Infructescences (cones) contained a mean of 12 follicles, holding two seeds of which 62% were estimated to be viable.

3 Cone (and seed) production increased with plant age to 15 years, but then fluctuated widely around a mean of 17 cones per year. By this time the average plant had an estimated canopy seed bank of 700 viable seeds comprising seeds 1-10 years old.

4 Seeds were lost from the canopy seed bank through spontaneous follicle rupture (i.e. in the absence of fire), granivory by insect larvae, and decay. Most follicles remained closed for at least 5 years and up to 50% of follicles were still closed after 10 years. Insect granivores destroyed 18% of seeds in 1-year-old cones, and continued to destroy seeds in older cones at a rate of 2-3% per year.

5 The seed bank model predicted continued seed accumulation in the canopy to at least age 25 years (1400 seeds), but by this time more viable seeds (≈ 2200) had been lost to spontaneous opening, granivory and decay than were then stored on the plant.

6 Shannon-Weiner diversity (H') of seed ages in the canopy seed bank increased with plant age, while evenness (V') decreased at first (to plant age 17 years) and then increased.

7 On a time-scale of many generations, the likelihood of successful recruitment of individuals in the next generation (on average), occurs for a fire frequency of 15-18 years. At this frequency resource wastage in this low-nutrient environment would be minimized.

8 Recent fires have recurred within 7-11 years and indicate a human impact on the natural fire regime which may ultimately threaten the species.

*Keywords*: *Banksia*, fire frequency, seed bank model, seed demography, serotiny

*Journal of Ecology* (1996) **84**, 9-17

#### Introduction

Serotiny refers to the retention of seeds in closed fruits within the plant canopy for more than one year, and can be contrasted with two alternative fates of seeds: storage in a soil seed bank, or release of short-lived seeds upon maturity (no seed storage) (Lamont et al. 1991a). Seed release in serotinous species is normally triggered by fire and seeds are short-lived after release, germinating during the first favourable period (Cowling & Lamont 1987). Species can range from weakly serotinous, where most seeds are released within a few years of production, to strongly serotinous, where seeds are held in the canopy for many years. The

ecological significance of serotiny seems clear: where conditions for seedling recruitment are best immediately following fire (i.e. competition for light, moisture and nutrients are probably at their minimum), cued release of canopy-stored seeds after fire maximizes the age, and therefore canopy seed store, of the population by the time of the next fire. Any seedlings that establish later during the interfire period have a low probability of survival due to competition with their parents and other established plants (Cowling & Lamont 1987; Lamont & Barker 1988). They will be much younger and, on average, will have a smaller canopy seed bank when fire recurs and so are less fit (*sensu* Stearns 1992).

The dynamics of seed production, storage and loss in relation to plant age determines the range of fire frequencies for which population maintenance is possible. If fire occurs either before the onset of reproductive maturity, or before a sufficient canopy seed bank has accumulated, then a population is threatened with extinction.

In the absence of fire some seeds are released by the spontaneous opening of old fruits, but the likelihood of plant recruitment and survival to reproductive age is extremely low. Seed release is hastened by the death of stem tissue due to drought stress and plant senescence (Witkowski et al. 1991). This means that the canopy seed bank may be completely lost where plant death occurs before the next fire, a fate not shared by most soil seed bank species where seeds may survive for many years after the death of parent plants (Baker 1989). Because dry plant biomass is more readily consumed by fire, any seeds held in the canopy of dead plants at the time of fire are also likely to perish (Lamont & Barker 1988).

*Banksia hookeriana* Meissn. (Proteaceae) is a highly serotinous, fire-killed (nonsprouting) woody shrub to 2.5 m high which is restricted to the northern sandplain scrub-heaths of south-western Australia about 250-330 km north of Perth (George 1981; Taylor & Hopper 1988). Seeds are held in a state of enforced dormancy within woody follicles on large infructescences (cones) in the crown. While new inflorescences may be damaged and removed from plants by birds, mature cones normally remain attached to the plant throughout its life. Some seeds abort during development, while others are either released gradually or (especially after fire) are consumed by insects, lose viability and decay, or remain viable. Once released seeds germinate with the onset of winter rains or perish as there is no persistent soil seed bank (Enright & Lamont 1989).

The geographical extent (80 × 30 km) of the low nutrient, noncalcareous, sandplain defines the distribution of this species, which is further limited by its specific preference for the deeper sands of low dune crests (Enright & Lamont 1989; Lamont et al. 1989). This means that the species exists as a large number of discrete populations of varying sizes (< 100 to > 10 000 individuals) separated by distances of 0.2 to > 1 km. The largest populations are located near Mt Adams in the northern part of the species range. Land clearance for agriculture, mining and mineral exploration, and increased incidence of anthropogenic ignition, make habitat loss and increased fire frequency potential threats to the long term survival of this species. In addition, its attractive orange inflorescences are harvested in large numbers for the commercial wildflower trade, so reducing seed production in exploited populations (Witkowski et al. 1994).

This paper describes seed production and availability, and a computer model of seed bank dynamics in *Banksia hookeriana* in relation to plant age (= time since last fire) for sites near Mt Adams. The following questions were posed:

1 What is the pattern of seed production with plant age, and what factors influence the rate of seed accumulation in the crown (e.g. level of serotiny, granivory, seed abortion and longevity)?

2 Does the analysis of seed demography reveal the optimum fire frequency to which the species is adapted, and the range of fire frequencies compatible with population survival?

#### STUDY AREA

The study was located in the Yardanogo Nature Reserve about 330 km north of Perth (29°25′S, 114°58′E). Mean annual rainfall at the two closest climate stations is 513 mm (Eneabba; 55 km to the south) and 471 mm (Dongara; 25 km to the north), respectively. There is a pronounced winter maximum with almost no rain (median 20 mm) in the five summer months from December to April. Temperature regimes are similar for both climate stations: mean maximum temperature in the hottest month (January) is 35.8 °C, mean minimum temperature in the coolest month (July) is 9.2 °C. Soils vary from acidic, leached sands on low dunes to sandy clays in intervening depressions (Hnatiuk & Hopkins 1981). The vegetation of the low dunes is a diverse scrub-heath usually dominated by two *Banksia* species, *Banksia hookeriana* and *Banksia attenuata* R. Br., although up to six banksias may co-occur (Beard 1984; Enright & Lamont 1989).

#### Materials and methods

Seven sample plots, each 400 m<sup>2</sup> in area and ranging in age since last fire from 1 to 3 and 14-16 years, were established in 1986 and monitored for 6-8 years. They were on the crests and slopes of low, sandy dunes in scrub-heath along the edge of a 2-km section of Mt Adams Road within the Yardanogo Nature Reserve. Sites covering a broader range of *Banksia hookeriana* stand ages could not be located.

For the five plots where plant age was 1-3 years at the start of the study, and when fire occurred subsequently during the study period (wildfire killed all plants in four of these five plots in 1991), age at time of last fire was estimated for 10 plants by the stem node ageing method described by Lamont (1985), or was known precisely. Seed production was estimated by counting the total number of cones on a random sample of 10 plants and the number of follicles on each of 10 randomly chosen cones per plant. The onset and level of flower head (inflorescence) and cone (infructescence) production were recorded within five replicate 25-m<sup>2</sup> subplots per plot for each year until 1991 (four plots) or 1993 (one plot).

For the two plots where plant age was 14-16 years in 1986, the total number of plants and total number of cones per plant was determined. For a random sample of 10 plants per plot, the height and crown diameter, and number of new cones was enumerated each year there-after until 1991 (when wildfire killed all plants in one plot) or 1993. Plots were searched each year for evidence of seedling establishment from spontaneous release of seeds in the absence of fire.

Complete cone crops were harvested from 10 randomly chosen 16-year-old plants at the start of the study in 1986. Cones were allocated to annual age classes using the stem node ageing method so that the entire history of reproduction could be determined for each plant. Degree of serotiny was based on the proportion of follicles per cone age class which had opened in the absence of fire (Cowling & Lamont 1985a). Cones were burned and subjected to wet-dry cycles to induce follicle rupture and facilitate seed removal (Cowling & Lamont 1985b). The numbers of follicles, and proportions of firm, aborted, eaten and decayed seeds were determined per plant by cone age. Viability of firm seeds was assessed by germinating batches of 25 seeds per cone age class from each of five plants (replicates) under moist conditions at 15 °C (Cowling et al. 1987).

#### STATISTICAL ANALYSES

Trends between seed parameters, plant age and cone age were analysed using regression models (SYSTAT 1992). Where data were not normally distributed, logarithmic (ln) and arcsine transformations were employed to satisfy assumptions of the regression models used. All error terms listed are standard errors.

A canopy seed bank dynamics model, written in programming language C++, was used to estimate the pattern of viable seed retention on plants and fate of seeds in relation to age. The model used regression equations and other statistics relating patterns of seed accumulation and loss to increasing plant and cone age. Shannon-Weiner diversity (H') and evenness (V') were calculated for the distribution of viable seed ages by plant age.

#### Results

#### CONE PRODUCTION

A few plants produced inflorescences at 3-4 years of age, but these were all sterile (age 3: mean inflorescences per plant = 0.12 ± 0.06; age 4: mean = 0.92 ± 0.23). Both within and between year variability in cone production per plant increased with plant age.

The total number of cones held in the crown increased continuously with plant age and although the standard error also increased with age, the mean pattern of accumulation showed a consistent trend (Fig. 1b, Table 1).

*Journal of Ecology* 1998, **86**, 946–959

# The ecological significance of canopy seed storage in fire-prone environments: a model for non-sprouting shrubs

NEAL J. ENRIGHT\*†, RALF MARSULA‡, BYRON B. LAMONT† and CHRISTIAN WISSEL‡

\*Department of Geography and Environmental Studies, University of Melbourne, Parkville 3052, Australia; †School of Environmental Biology, Curtin University of Technology, GPO Box U1987 Perth 6001, Australia; and ‡Department of Ecological Modelling, UFZ Centre for Environmental Research, Leipzig-Halle, Permoserstr. 15, PF 2, D-04301 Leipzig, Germany

# Summary

1 A comprehensive data set on age, survival and reproduction for the non-sprouting (fire-killed) shrub *Banksia hookeriana*, encompassing 13 years of measurements at 15 sites in south-western Australia, and including 10 fires, was used to parameterize a computer model to investigate optimum plant life-history strategies in a fire-prone environment. Parameter ranges encompassed life-history information for other non-sprouting Banksia species from the same region.

2 The relationship between fire interval and level of canopy seed storage (serotiny) was analysed to identify the circumstances under which serotiny is favoured, and what degree of serotiny maximizes potential population growth rate. In addition to deterministic versions of the model, stochasticity in fire interval and conditions for recruitment were analysed.

3 The deterministic model indicated a maximum finite rate of natural increase (λ = 1.15) when the fire interval was 16 years and all seeds were retained on the plant until fire occurred. Although the model failed to predict the intermediate degrees of serotiny present in nature, it supported the optimum fire interval predicted from canopy seed bank dynamics.

4 Changes to biological attributes associated with timing of reproduction and longevity shifted the optimum fire interval and estimated rate of population growth, but did not alter the conclusions concerning serotiny. Although shorter seed longevity and increased rates of predation and/or decay reduced the value of serotiny, even very low levels of canopy seed storage increased species fitness under intermediate fire frequencies (10–20 years).

5 If the probability of inter-fire recruitment and survival was increased, optimum growth shifted from strong serotiny under a regime of frequent fire (<20 year interval), to weak (or no) serotiny where the interval between successive fires was long (>40 year interval).

6 Stochasticity around mean fire interval resulted in intermediate to strong (but not complete) serotiny being predicted as optimal once the CV for fire interval approached 100%. This result is interpreted as a bet-hedging strategy whereby spontaneous release of some seeds during the inter-fire period permits recruitment on rare occasions where fire interval approaches or exceeds the species longevity.

*Keywords: Banksia*, computer models, fire regime, optimum life-history strategies, serotiny, stochastic effects, woody plants

*Journal of Ecology* (1998) **86**, 946–959

946 Correspondence: Dr Neal Enright (fax 61 3 9344 4972; e-mail enright@ariel.ucs.unimelb.edu.au).



=====PAGE 2


947 *N.J. Enright* et al.

# Introduction

Plants in fire-prone environments are often characterized by biological attributes that increase the probability of survival and/or recruitment following disturbance by fire. Among these are the ability of individuals to regrow from protected buds either above- or below-ground (resprouting), fire-stimulated flowering and seed production, and fire-triggered germination of seeds stored either in the soil or in the plant canopy (Gill 1981). Since species that resprout after fire commonly co-exist in fire-prone environments (e.g. mediterranean-type shrublands) with those that are killed by fire (non-sprouters), a frequent question concerns the circumstances under which one or other strategy is favoured (e.g. Keeley & Zedler 1978; Keeley 1986; Hilbert 1987). Beyond this simple dichotomous division into resprouters and non-sprouters, fire-prone communities may contain an array of (sometimes congeneric) species showing consistent variation in the amount of resprouting after fire, the extent to which seeds are stored in the soil or on the plant, and in other biological attributes (e.g. longevity, age to reproduction, level of seed production).

It is important to determine the biological attributes that influence demographic behaviour and to establish which attributes confer the greatest fitness advantage on a species in relation to particular fire regimes. As well as revealing information on the selective pressures acting on species in fire-prone environments, the answers aid conservation and management of species in relation to human-imposed fire regimes.

This paper presents a computer model of population dynamics for a non-sprouting woody perennial in a fire-prone environment, and the results of simulations which sought to reveal the optimum level of on-plant seed storage (serotiny) in relation to fire interval. Serotiny refers to the retention of seeds in closed fruits or cones within the crown for more than 1 year and is common in species from a number of important families in fire-prone areas of Australia (Proteaceae, Myrtaceae, Cupressaceae, Casuarinaceae), South Africa (Proteaceae, Bruniaceae) and North America (Pinaceae) (Lamont et al. 1991a). It can be contrasted with two alternative fates of seeds: storage in a soil seed bank, or release of short-lived seeds once mature (no seed storage). Seed release in serotinous species is normally triggered by fire and seeds are short-lived after release, germinating during the first favourable period (Cowling & Lamont 1987). Species can range from weakly serotinous, where most seeds are released spontaneously (in the absence of fire) within a few years of production, to strongly serotinous, where most seeds are held in the canopy for many years (e.g. >10 years in some species of Pinus and Banksia).

The ecological and evolutionary significance of serotiny seems clear: where fire is the most common cause of ecosystem disturbance, cued release of canopy-stored seeds by fire (and their germination in the first growing season after fire) maximizes plant age and therefore seed available for the next generation by the time of the next fire. Seeds released, and seedlings established, later during the inter-fire period have a lower probability of survival due to competition with their parents and other established plants (Cowling & Lamont 1987). They will be younger and will thus have a smaller canopy seed bank when fire recurs, and so are less fit (sensu Stearns 1992). It would therefore appear that very strong serotiny should represent the optimum strategy for perennial plants in fire-prone environments. However, a range of degrees of serotiny may be encountered within the same plant community (e.g. Cowling et al. 1987; Enright & Lamont 1989a,b) or even within the same species. In the latter case, variations have been found in relation to environmental gradients, e.g. lower serotiny in less fire-prone parts of the species’ geographical range for *Banksia attenuata* in Australia (Cowling & Lamont 1985), and in relation to time since last fire, e.g. inter-fire recruits show lower serotiny than immediate post-fire recruits of *Pinus banksiana* in boreal forests of southern Quebec (Gautier et al. 1996). Lamont et al. (1991a) note that some fire regimes and growth forms apparently foster incomplete serotiny, but that ‘degree of serotiny has received little formal treatment, and the empirical subtleties of such relationships remain largely unexplored’.

The model described here is based on field data collected over 13 years from 15 sites and including 10 different fires (up to two at the same site) for *B. hookeriana* Meissn. (Proteaceae), a non-sprouting woody shrub of mediterranean-type shrublands in south-western Australia (Enright & Lamont 1989a, 1992a,b; Enright et al. 1996). Nevertheless, the model is likely to have a more general application since parameter values can readily be changed to match the known life-history attributes of other serotinous, non-sprouting perennial plants. By basing the model and its parameter values on those measured over an extended period of time (and at a number of sites) for a real plant species the model described here avoids many of the criticisms levelled at population models. For example, Cousens (1995) argues that the results of simulation studies for hypothetical species are often determined largely by the structure of the models themselves and provide little insight into real population dynamic behaviour and, further, that many models based on real data are flawed since the data are derived from glasshouse experiments or from density studies that exclude stochastic year-to-year variations in factors unrelated to density (e.g. weather).



=====PAGE 3


948 Canopy seed storage in non-sprouting shrubs

#### Ecological and biological attributes of *B. hookeriana*

#### FIELD DATA COLLECTION

*Banksia hookeriana* is a highly serotinous, fire-killed (non-sprouting) woody shrub that grows up to 2.5 m in height, which is restricted to the northern sandplain heaths of south-western Australia (centred on 29°30′S, 115°15′E) about 250–330 km north of Perth (George 1981; Taylor & Hopper 1988). Seed production and plant survivorship were estimated for sample populations of different ages (i.e. time since last fire). Sites covering the whole range of possible plant ages could not be located, and fires during the course of remeasurements returned some sites to zero age. Fifteen sample plots, each 400 m<sup>2</sup> in area, and ranging in age from 1 to 16 years at the start of the study, were established and censused annually in June (i.e. at the end of the summer–autumn period of peak plant mortality) from 1986 to 1996.

The onset and level of flowering (inflorescence) and cone (infructescence) production were recorded for all individuals within five replicate 25 m<sup>2</sup> subplots per plot for stands <8 years old, and annual cone production followed for a random sample of 10 individuals for older stands. Fertile cones typically carry 5–15 woody follicles arranged around a central rachis, each follicle holding two seeds. Cones arise terminally at the beginning of each growing season, and node scars and branching pattern clearly mark the boundary between successive years of vegetative growth. Thus plant age and individual cone age can be determined with only a small likelihood of error. Complete cone crops were harvested from 20 randomly chosen 16-year-old plants in 1986, and cones were aged so that the entire history of reproduction could be determined for each plant. The numbers of firm, aborted, eaten and decayed seeds in closed follicles were determined by cone age, and viability of firm seeds was assessed by germination testing (full details are provided in Enright et al. 1996). Degree of serotiny was based on the proportion of follicles per cone age class that remained closed in the absence of fire (following Lamont et al. 1991a).

The total number of cones per plant was quantified for all plants in plots affected by wild fires during the course of the field study. The number of follicles opened by fire was enumerated for a random sample of 10 cones on each of 10 plant skeletons per plot, and the number of viable seeds released per plant estimated using data for seeds from harvested cones.

Plant survivorship was recorded annually for 10 randomly chosen individuals within each subplot where plant age was <8 years, and in the whole plot for older stands. The number of seeds released following fire, the number of seedlings established in the first winter, and number of survivors at each age was used to produce survivorship trajectories. These trajectories described the number of seeds required to produce a new individual of any particular age.

Data for three other non-sprouting Banksia species (*B. prionotes* Lindley, *B. leptophylla* A.S. George and *B. lanata* A.S. George) provided information on ranges for parameter values for modelling purposes. Up to six Banksia species (a mixture of resprouters and non-sprouters) co-occurred in some of the field sites. The biological attributes of these species are described in Cowling et al. (1987), Enright & Lamont (1989a) and Enright & Lamont (1992a).

#### SPECIES ATTRIBUTES

Seed production typically commences when plants are 5 years old and fluctuates widely around a mean of about 200 viable seeds per year from 15 years onwards (Enright et al. 1996). While new inflorescences may be damaged and removed from plants by birds, mature cones normally remain attached to the plant throughout their life. Few seeds are released except when fire causes the follicles on cones to open. Once released, seeds either germinate with the onset of winter rains or perish (Enright & Lamont 1989a). Enright et al. (1996) describe in detail the mean rate of accumulation of viable seeds in the canopy in relation to plant age. On average, 17% of embryos abort; seed losses due to spontaneous release in the absence of fire average 4% per annum; while predation and decay of seeds stored in closed follicles increases by 4% per annum from the first year.

From 3% to 27% of seeds released following fires in the period 1985–93 produced seedlings in the first winter (Enright & Lamont 1989a; N. J. Enright, unpublished data). Plant survivorship is lowest in the first year and quickly increases such that there is little mortality (<1% year<sup>−1</sup>) in plants older than 8 years. While no plants older than 25 years have been observed in the field, the continuing survival of most individuals in our oldest study site (N. J. Enright, unpublished data) indicates that longevity may be 30–40 years in the absence of fire. Large, old plants may succumb to drought over summer, and are prone to collapse due to the heavy load of seed-bearing cones on old branches, and this suggests an increased mortality rate for old plants.

In the absence of fire, some seeds are released by the spontaneous opening of old fruits, but the probability of germination and survival of recruits to reproductive age is extremely low. Seedlings are occasionally encountered in stands >15 years old, but so far no such recruits have been recorded to survive to reproductive age. Nevertheless, it is reasonable to assume that occasionally these inter-fire recruits might grow to maturity and contribute to future generations. The low chance of establishment, combined with low rates of seed release when the degree of serotiny is high, means that very few recruits are likely via this pathway.



=====PAGE 4


949 *N.J. Enright* et al.

Seed release is hastened by the death of stem tissues due to drought stress and plant senescence, but is incomplete relative to seed release after fire (Witkowski et al. 1991). The canopy seed bank may be completely lost where plant death occurs before the next fire, both because even if seeds are released they will have a low probability of establishment, and because dead plants are usually completely incinerated by fire so that any seeds still held in the crown will perish (Lamont & Barker 1988). The woody stems and cones on living shrubs burn less intensely due to a higher moisture content, and although the stems are killed they remain standing and the cones are opened but not consumed. If fire occurs either before the onset of reproductive maturity, or before a sufficient canopy seed bank has accumulated, a population is threatened with local extinction.

### WEATHER AND FIRE

Mediterranean-type climate regions are characterized by cool, moist winters and hot, dry summers. In the northern sandplain heaths of south-western Australia, winter rains are highly predictable and will almost always provide sufficient moisture to allow seedling establishment after fire. However, the extent of summer drought is more variable. One-hundred and ten years of rainfall records for nearby Dongara (Western Australian Bureau of Meteorology climate station 8044; 29°15′S, 114°56′E, mean annual rainfall of 471 mm for the period 1884–1993) show that about 80% of summers have the typical mediterranean-type pattern of low to very low rainfall. In the other 20% of years, tropical storms punctuate the summer with heavy rainfall events and drought stress on plants is greatly reduced (Enright & Lamont 1992a).

Summer weather conditions are important in determining levels of seedling survival in the first year following fire. Survivorship of seedlings is highest in wet summers and lowest in dry summers (Enright & Lamont 1992a). There was no relationship between rainfall in the previous summer and subsequent inflorescence production for plants >15 years old. However, there was a significant positive relationship between total rainfall in one year and inflorescence production in the next (log<sub>10</sub> cones = 5.45 × log<sub>10</sub> annual rainfall – 13.80; d.f. = 16, F = 10.50, P < 0.05, r<sup>2</sup> = 0.36). This non-linear relationship suggests reduced inflorescence production following years of lower than average rainfall, but little increase above average levels of production following wet years.

Risk of fire is high every summer and there is no obvious relationship between rainfall and fire: of nine wild fires recorded in the vicinity of the field area since 1967, four occurred in wetter than average years, and four in years with very dry summers (one of which followed a wet winter). However, the timing of fire in relation to rainfall in the first few years after fire (especially unusually wet or dry summers) is important since seedling mortality is highest during this period (Enright & Lamont 1989a, 1992a). Stands burned within the last 5 years are unlikely to have accumulated sufficient biomass to carry a fire. The shortest recorded fire interval in relation to the nine fires noted above was 7 years.

# Methods

### THE MODEL

The computer model, written in C++, describes the population dynamics of a serotinous, non-sprouting woody perennial that is subject to disturbance by fire. We chose an age-based approach to characterize the population: the model traces the number of x-year-old plants, N(x), and the number of seeds stored on an x-year-old plant, S(x), for each age x. Changes in N(x) and S(x) are caused by plant death, seed production, seed loss, seed release, germination and establishment of seedlings. These processes are described by the functional relationships detailed below, and illustrated conceptually in Fig. 1. The model begins with a post-fire population of 100 viable seeds and calculates their survivorship and reproduction in relation to age until fire causes plant death and seed release. Fire kills all individuals, and recruitment following fire is solely from seeds.

Germination, establishment and survivorship of plants depend on the growing conditions (especially summer rainfall), and the model uses the fits derived from field data on survivorship, and illustrated in Fig. 2, to describe these rates. The probability of germination of seeds and establishment of seedlings in the first year is the inverse of the observed number of seeds required for self-replacement of a 1-year-old plant. In the same way, the probability p(x) that a plant survives until it is x years old is the inverse of the number of seeds required for self-replacement of a plant at age x. Thus, the probability p(x, x + 1) to survive from year x to year x + 1 can be calculated

Fig. 1 Summary flow diagram of the main processes built into the computer model for a serotinous, non-sprouting perennial plant. Note this is not a complete flow diagram of the model. Full model details are described in the text.

In the latter case, variations have been found in relation to environmental gradients, e.g. lower serotiny in less fire-prone parts of the species’ geographical range for *Banksia attenuata* in Australia (Cowling & Lamont 1985), and in relation to time since last fire, e.g. inter-fire recruits show lower serotiny than immediate post-fire recruits of *Pinus banksiana* in boreal forests of southern Quebec (Gautier et al. 1996). Lamont et al. (1991a) note that some fire regimes and growth forms apparently foster incomplete serotiny, but that ‘degree of serotiny has received little formal treatment, and the empirical subtleties of such relationships remain largely unexplored’.

The model described here is based on field data collected over 13 years from 15 sites and including 10 different fires (up to two at the same site) for *B. hookeriana* Meissn. (Proteaceae), a non-sprouting woody shrub of mediterranean-type shrublands in south-western Australia (Enright & Lamont 1989a, 1992a,b; Enright et al. 1996). Nevertheless, the model is likely to have a more general application since parameter values can readily be changed to match the known life-history attributes of other serotinous, non-sprouting perennial plants. By basing the model and its parameter values on those measured over an extended period of time (and at a number of sites) for a real plant species the model described here avoids many of the criticisms levelled at population models. For example, Cousens (1995) argues that the results of simulation studies for hypothetical species are often determined largely by the structure of the models themselves and provide little insight into real population dynamic behaviour and, further, that many models based on real data are flawed since the data are derived from glasshouse experiments or from density studies that exclude stochastic year-to-year variations in factors unrelated to density (e.g. weather).



=====PAGE 3


948 Canopy seed storage in non-sprouting shrubs

#### Ecological and biological attributes of *B. hookeriana*

#### FIELD DATA COLLECTION

*Banksia hookeriana* is a highly serotinous, fire-killed (non-sprouting) woody shrub that grows up to 2.5 m in height, which is restricted to the northern sandplain heaths of south-western Australia (centred on 29°30′S, 115°15′E) about 250–330 km north of Perth (George 1981; Taylor & Hopper 1988). Seed production and plant survivorship were estimated for sample populations of different ages (i.e. time since last fire). Sites covering the whole range of possible plant ages could not be located, and fires during the course of remeasurements returned some sites to zero age. Fifteen sample plots, each 400 m<sup>2</sup> in area, and ranging in age from 1 to 16 years at the start of the study, were established and censused annually in June (i.e. at the end of the summer–autumn period of peak plant mortality) from 1986 to 1996.

The onset and level of flowering (inflorescence) and cone (infructescence) production were recorded for all individuals within five replicate 25 m<sup>2</sup> subplots per plot for stands <8 years old, and annual cone production followed for a random sample of 10 individuals for older stands. Fertile cones typically carry 5–15 woody follicles arranged around a central rachis, each follicle holding two seeds. Cones arise terminally at the beginning of each growing season, and node scars and branching pattern clearly mark the boundary between successive years of vegetative growth. Thus plant age and individual cone age can be determined with only a small likelihood of error. Complete cone crops were harvested from 20 randomly chosen 16-year-old plants in 1986, and cones were aged so that the entire history of reproduction could be determined for each plant. The numbers of firm, aborted, eaten and decayed seeds in closed follicles were determined by cone age, and viability of firm seeds was assessed by germination testing (full details are provided in Enright et al. 1996). Degree of serotiny was based on the proportion of follicles per cone age class that remained closed in the absence of fire (following Lamont et al. 1991a).

The total number of cones per plant was quantified for all plants in plots affected by wild fires during the course of the field study. The number of follicles opened by fire was enumerated for a random sample of 10 cones on each of 10 plant skeletons per plot, and the number of viable seeds released per plant estimated using data for seeds from harvested cones.

Plant survivorship was recorded annually for 10 randomly chosen individuals within each subplot where plant age was <8 years, and in the whole plot for older stands. The number of seeds released following fire, the number of seedlings established in the first winter, and number of survivors at each age was used to produce survivorship trajectories. These trajectories described the number of seeds required to produce a new individual of any particular age.

Data for three other non-sprouting Banksia species (*B. prionotes* Lindley, *B. leptophylla* A.S. George and *B. lanata* A.S. George) provided information on ranges for parameter values for modelling purposes. Up to six Banksia species (a mixture of resprouters and non-sprouters) co-occurred in some of the field sites. The biological attributes of these species are described in Cowling et al. (1987), Enright & Lamont (1989a) and Enright & Lamont (1992a).

#### SPECIES ATTRIBUTES

Seed production typically commences when plants are 5 years old and fluctuates widely around a mean of about 200 viable seeds per year from 15 years onwards (Enright et al. 1996). While new inflorescences may be damaged and removed from plants by birds, mature cones normally remain attached to the plant throughout their life. Few seeds are released except when fire causes the follicles on cones to open. Once released, seeds either germinate with the onset of winter rains or perish (Enright & Lamont 1989a). Enright et al. (1996) describe in detail the mean rate of accumulation of viable seeds in the canopy in relation to plant age. On average, 17% of embryos abort; seed losses due to spontaneous release in the absence of fire average 4% per annum; while predation and decay of seeds stored in closed follicles increases by 4% per annum from the first year.

From 3% to 27% of seeds released following fires in the period 1985–93 produced seedlings in the first winter (Enright & Lamont 1989a; N. J. Enright, unpublished data). Plant survivorship is lowest in the first year and quickly increases such that there is little mortality (<1% year<sup>−1</sup>) in plants older than 8 years. While no plants older than 25 years have been observed in the field, the continuing survival of most individuals in our oldest study site (N. J. Enright, unpublished data) indicates that longevity may be 30–40 years in the absence of fire. Large, old plants may succumb to drought over summer, and are prone to collapse due to the heavy load of seed-bearing cones on old branches, and this suggests an increased mortality rate for old plants.

In the absence of fire, some seeds are released by the spontaneous opening of old fruits, but the probability of germination and survival of recruits to reproductive age is extremely low. Seedlings are occasionally encountered in stands >15 years old, but so far no such recruits have been recorded to survive to reproductive age. Nevertheless, it is reasonable to assume that occasionally these inter-fire recruits might grow to maturity and contribute to future generations. The low chance of establishment, combined with low rates of seed release when the degree of serotiny is high, means that very few recruits are likely via this pathway.



=====PAGE 4


949 *N.J. Enright* et al.

Seed release is hastened by the death of stem tissues due to drought stress and plant senescence, but is incomplete relative to seed release after fire (Witkowski et al. 1991). The canopy seed bank may be completely lost where plant death occurs before the next fire, both because even if seeds are released they will have a low probability of establishment, and because dead plants are usually completely incinerated by fire so that any seeds still held in the crown will perish (Lamont & Barker 1988). The woody stems and cones on living shrubs burn less intensely due to a higher moisture content, and although the stems are killed they remain standing and the cones are opened but not consumed. If fire occurs either before the onset of reproductive maturity, or before a sufficient canopy seed bank has accumulated, a population is threatened with local extinction.

### WEATHER AND FIRE

Mediterranean-type climate regions are characterized by cool, moist winters and hot, dry summers. In the northern sandplain heaths of south-western Australia, winter rains are highly predictable and will almost always provide sufficient moisture to allow seedling establishment after fire. However, the extent of summer drought is more variable. One-hundred and ten years of rainfall records for nearby Dongara (Western Australian Bureau of Meteorology climate station 8044; 29°15′S, 114°56′E, mean annual rainfall of 471 mm for the period 1884–1993) show that about 80% of summers have the typical mediterranean-type pattern of low to very low rainfall. In the other 20% of years, tropical storms punctuate the summer with heavy rainfall events and drought stress on plants is greatly reduced (Enright & Lamont 1992a).

Summer weather conditions are important in determining levels of seedling survival in the first year following fire. Survivorship of seedlings is highest in wet summers and lowest in dry summers (Enright & Lamont 1992a). There was no relationship between rainfall in the previous summer and subsequent inflorescence production for plants >15 years old. However, there was a significant positive relationship between total rainfall in one year and inflorescence production in the next (log<sub>10</sub> cones = 5.45 × log<sub>10</sub> annual rainfall – 13.80; d.f. = 16, F = 10.50, P < 0.05, r<sup>2</sup> = 0.36). This non-linear relationship suggests reduced inflorescence production following years of lower than average rainfall, but little increase above average levels of production following wet years.

Risk of fire is high every summer and there is no obvious relationship between rainfall and fire: of nine wild fires recorded in the vicinity of the field area since 1967, four occurred in wetter than average years, and four in years with very dry summers (one of which followed a wet winter). However, the timing of fire in relation to rainfall in the first few years after fire (especially unusually wet or dry summers) is important since seedling mortality is highest during this period (Enright & Lamont 1989a, 1992a). Stands burned within the last 5 years are unlikely to have accumulated sufficient biomass to carry a fire. The shortest recorded fire interval in relation to the nine fires noted above was 7 years.

# Methods

### THE MODEL

The computer model, written in C++, describes the population dynamics of a serotinous, non-sprouting woody perennial that is subject to disturbance by fire. We chose an age-based approach to characterize the population: the model traces the number of x-year-old plants, N(x), and the number of seeds stored on an x-year-old plant, S(x), for each age x. Changes in N(x) and S(x) are caused by plant death, seed production, seed loss, seed release, germination and establishment of seedlings. These processes are described by the functional relationships detailed below, and illustrated conceptually in Fig. 1. The model begins with a post-fire population of 100 viable seeds and calculates their survivorship and reproduction in relation to age until fire causes plant death and seed release. Fire kills all individuals, and recruitment following fire is solely from seeds.

Germination, establishment and survivorship of plants depend on the growing conditions (especially summer rainfall), and the model uses the fits derived from field data on survivorship, and illustrated in Fig. 2, to describe these rates. The probability of germination of seeds and establishment of seedlings in the first year is the inverse of the observed number of seeds required for self-replacement of a 1-year-old plant. In the same way, the probability p(x) that a plant survives until it is x years old is the inverse of the number of seeds required for self-replacement of a plant at age x.
